§2.2 Lagrangians

2.2 Lagrangians

.

2.2.1 Lagrangians

Definition 2.2.1.1 (Lagrangian).

The Lagrangian (Density) ℒ︀, similar to the Hamiltonian 𝐻 (or ℋ︀ for Hamiltonian density, defined as 𝐻=∫d3𝑥ℋ︀) as they both can be used to describe the evolution of a system. In Field Theories, densities are used more commonly. The Density of either quantity, as stated before, is a more useful quantity in Field theories due to Lorentz Invariance and other such things.

Definition 2.2.1.2 (Action).

Action 𝑆 is defined as

𝑆=∫d𝑡𝐿=∫d4𝑥ℒ︀
which should be familiar from studying classical mechanics (Lagrangian mechanics specifically). This quantity is minimized in order to obtain the evolution of a system (Equations of Motion).

Theorem 2.2.1.3 (Euler Lagrange Equations).

In order to minimize the action of a system with Lagrangian Density ℒ︀[𝜙,𝜕𝜇𝜙], the system must satisfy the Euler Lagrange Equations:

𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)=0
A differential equation which ends up being extremely useful in physics for describing the time evolution of a system.

Proof.

We aim to equate the variation of the action 𝑆 with respect to the field 𝜙 to zero. That is, we require

𝛿𝑆𝛿𝜙=0

Note that

𝑆=∫d𝑡𝐿=∫d4𝑥ℒ︀[𝜙,𝜕𝜇𝜙]

in order to obtain 𝛿𝑆, we must perform a transformation 𝜙→𝜙+𝛿𝜙 in the Lagrangian. This provides

𝛿𝑆=∫𝑑4𝑥(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙𝛿𝜙+𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜇𝜙))

Via the product rule and the fact that infinitesimal variations commute with partial derivatives1, we have that

𝛿𝑆=∫d4𝑥(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙𝛿𝜙+𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙)−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙)𝛿𝑆=∫d4𝑥(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙𝛿𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙+𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙))𝛿𝑆=∫d4𝑥((𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))𝛿𝜙+𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙))

Now we need to prove that the final term (the one without the shared common factor of 𝛿𝜙) vanishes as our integration bounds become infinite (as we are integrating over all spacetime of course). Since this term is a total derivative of some quantity that we will define to be

𝐴𝜇≡𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙

(Something similar with the form of 𝐴𝜇𝛿𝛼 is a physically important quantity but this 𝐴𝜇 is not of any significance besides being useful for math). With the derivative being of course 𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇. The integral of this quantity is

∫d4𝑥𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇

and by the 4 dimensional divergence theorem, we obtain

∫𝑉d4𝑥𝜕𝜇𝐴𝜇=∮𝜕𝑉d3𝜎𝜇𝐴𝜇

This must vanish, given that the 𝛿𝜙 is forced to vanish at the boundaries by the principle of least action. Therefore, we have that

𝛿𝑆𝛿𝜙=∫d4𝑥(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))=0

For the integral to vanish, the integrand must vanish, therefore

𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)=0

⁠□

Theorem 2.2.1.4 (Extended Euler Lagrange Equations).

In order to minimize the action of a system with Lagrangian Density ℒ︀[𝜙,𝜕𝜇𝜙,𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙,…], the system must satisfy the Extended Euler Lagrange Equations:

𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)+𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)−⋯=0

(This was actually a problem in the Schwartz QFT textbook, so if you are reading that, potentially skip this part.)

Proof.

We begin in a similar way to the proof to the Euler-Lagrange equations.

𝛿𝑆=∫d4𝑥(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙𝛿𝜙+𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜇𝜙)+𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)+⋯)

We then utilize the product rule (or the reverse of it) to obtain

𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙)=𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙+ 𝜕𝜈𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜇𝜙)+𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜈𝜙)+𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)

We can rewrite 𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜈𝜙) and 𝜕𝜈𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿(𝜕𝜇𝜙) via similar methods and we can continue to do so with more terms forming a pattern of the 𝑛th (with 𝑛 partial derivatives) term has a coefficient of (−1)𝑛 (this method similar to the principle of inclusion-exclusion)

𝛿𝑆=∫d4𝑥((𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)+𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)−⋯)𝛿𝜙+𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙)+𝜕𝜇(𝜕𝜈𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)𝛿𝜙)+𝜕𝜈(𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇)𝛿𝜙)+𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜈(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜈)𝛿𝜙)+⋯)

Every term besides those with the shared factor of 𝛿𝜙 disappears due to similar reasons mentioned in the proof of the Euler-Lagrange equations (i.e. they are total derivatives). and therefore, since we want 𝛿𝑆𝛿𝜙=0, we have that

𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)+𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜈𝜕𝜇𝜙)−⋯=0

⁠□

Example 2.2.1.5 (Lagrangian).

An example of a Lagrangian that can apply to some general scalar field 𝜙2 is the Lagrangian

ℒ︀=12(𝜕𝜇𝜙)(𝜕𝜇𝜙)−𝑉[𝜙]

This would give us the equation of motion

𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙)=0−𝑉′[𝜙]−□𝜙=0

so

(□+𝑉′[𝜙])𝜙=0

which is related to the Klein-Gordon equation (□+𝑚2)𝜙=0.

  • One can split the terms of a Lagrangian ℒ︀ into Kinetic terms and Interacting terms.

    • Kinetic terms of a Lagrangian are ones which have at most 2 fields in it

      • ℒ︀kin⊃12𝜙□𝜙,𝜓̄𝜕𝜓,14𝐹𝜇𝜈2,12𝑚2𝜙2,⋯
  • Interacting terms are terms with more than 2 fields
ℒ︀int⊃𝜆𝜙3,𝑔𝜓̄𝐴𝜓,𝑔𝜕𝜇𝜙𝐴𝜇𝜙⋆,⋯

Remark.

Interacting terms in the lagrangian all have a factor 𝜆 or 𝑔 associated with them. This is due to the fact that it is a coupling constant related to the interaction.
